note:
Hospital day 2 for a 42-year-old male admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. He presented with 3 days of nausea, headache, and progressive confusion, and his wife reported that he was unsteady on his feet. His history includes depression and hypertension. Sertraline was increased from 50 mg to 100 mg daily about 3 weeks ago, and he also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. He does not drink alcohol excessively and reports normal fluid intake at home.

Admission serum sodium was 118 mEq/L. He received two boluses of 3% saline, 100 mL each, on the night of admission, with improvement in his headache and mental status. There were no further overnight events. This morning he reports that the headache has resolved and the nausea is mild, and he feels clearer. He denies vomiting, seizure, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

Vitals this morning: BP 128/78, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 98.4 F. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time with no focal neurologic deficit. Mucous membranes are moist, there is no peripheral edema or jugular venous distension, and the lungs are clear. He appears euvolemic.

Serum sodium trended from 118 to 121 at 6 hours and 124 this morning, a rise of 6 mEq/L over about 24 hours, which is within the safe correction limit. Serum osmolality was low at 252 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality was inappropriately high at 480 mOsm/kg. The urine sodium concentration was elevated. TSH and morning cortisol were normal. Glucose 96 and creatinine 0.9.

Impression is euvolemic hyponatremia most consistent with SIADH from the recent sertraline dose increase. Depression is currently stable and hypertension is well controlled.

Sertraline is stopped today and psychiatry will be consulted to choose an alternative antidepressant. Start fluid restriction to 1 L per day. Repeat serum sodium every six hours, with a goal of no more than an 8 mEq/L rise in 24 hours. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. Start ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea. If the sodium is 130 or higher tomorrow, plan discharge with a repeat basic metabolic panel in 1 week with his primary care physician.

His history includes depression and hypertension, and sertraline was recently increased to 100 mg daily. Admission serum sodium was 118 mEq/L and rose to 124 after two boluses of 3% saline, and he is euvolemic with low serum osmolality and high urine osmolality. The impression is SIADH from the sertraline increase. Sertraline is stopped, psychiatry will advise on an alternative, fluid restriction and serial sodium checks are started, amlodipine continues, and ondansetron is added for nausea.

note:
Postoperative day 1 for a 72-year-old female who underwent arthroscopic repair of a full-thickness right supraspinatus rotator cuff tear yesterday. The tear developed after a fall on an outstretched arm 6 weeks ago, and she had persistent night pain and weakness with overhead reaching despite physical therapy. She has hypertension, which has been well controlled.

She slept in the recliner overnight and reports shoulder pain of 4 out of 10 this morning, controlled on her current regimen. She denies numbness or tingling in the hand, nausea, fever, and chest pain. She has been eating breakfast and walked in the hallway with nursing.

Vitals: BP 132/76, HR 72, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 98.2 F. The right arm is in an abduction sling. The dressings are clean, dry, and intact with no drainage or surrounding erythema. Swelling is mild. The hand is warm with brisk capillary refill, and sensation and finger movement are intact. The interscalene block has worn off.

Impression is a stable postoperative course after rotator cuff repair with adequately controlled pain.

Continue acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours scheduled and oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for breakthrough pain. She will keep the sling on at all times except for hygiene and pendulum exercises. Discharge home today with a follow-up visit in the orthopedic clinic in 2 weeks for a wound check and to start the physical therapy protocol. She was told to call for fever, increasing pain, redness, or numbness.

Pain is 4 out of 10 and controlled, and she denies numbness, tingling, nausea, fever, and chest pain. Vitals are stable, the dressings are clean and dry, and hand sensation and finger movement are intact. The impression is a stable postoperative course. She continues acetaminophen and oxycodone as needed, stays in the sling, and will be discharged today with orthopedic clinic follow-up in 2 weeks for a wound check and physical therapy.

Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 71-year-old male here to review your blood sugar and weight. Your primary care doctor sent you because your A1c has been creeping up. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, doc. I am a little tired in the afternoons, and I have gained some weight around the belly over the last two years.
Doctor: Any increased thirst or urinating more than usual?
Patient: No, nothing like that. No blurry vision either.
Doctor: What about numbness or tingling in your feet, or chest pain with walking?
Patient: No numbness in my feet and no chest pain. I walk the dog most days.
Doctor: Good. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take atorvastatin 20 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, and a baby aspirin 81 mg each morning.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Yes, lisinopril. I got swelling of my lips and tongue about five years ago, and they told me it was angioedema. I was told never to take it again.
Doctor: Thank you. I will keep that on your chart as an allergy to lisinopril with angioedema, so no ACE inhibitors for you.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Let me go through your numbers. Today your blood pressure is 138/84, heart rate 72, weight 228 pounds, and BMI 33. Your waist measures 112 centimeters. Your heart sounds regular, the lungs are clear, and your feet have normal sensation on the monofilament test with good pulses. The labs from last week show hemoglobin A1c 6.2 percent, fasting glucose 112, triglycerides 210, HDL 36, LDL 84, and creatinine 1.0 with an eGFR of 78.
Patient: So am I diabetic?
Doctor: Not yet. You have prediabetes, and together with the belly fat, high triglycerides, low HDL, and elevated blood pressure, this is metabolic syndrome. It raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, but it is very treatable.
Patient: What should I do?
Doctor: The most important step is lifestyle. I would like you to aim for 150 minutes of walking a week, cut back on sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, and see our dietitian. I am also starting metformin 500 mg once a day with dinner, and we will increase it slowly if your stomach tolerates it. Your kidney function is fine for it. I am increasing amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily because your pressure is above goal, and I will send a note to your primary care doctor. Please keep taking the atorvastatin and the aspirin. Do not take any ACE inhibitor. We will repeat the A1c and a lipid panel in three months.
Patient: Sounds fair. Should I check my sugar at home?
Doctor: Not needed right now. Come back in three months.
summary: A 71-year-old male with rising A1c was seen for prediabetes and metabolic syndrome; he reports afternoon tiredness and abdominal weight gain and denies increased thirst, blurry vision, numbness in his feet, and chest pain. He has a documented allergy to lisinopril with angioedema. Blood pressure was 138/84, BMI 33, A1c 6.2 percent, triglycerides 210, and HDL 36. The assessment is prediabetes with metabolic syndrome. Metformin is started, amlodipine is increased to 10 mg daily, an ACE inhibitor is to be avoided, and lifestyle changes, dietitian referral, and repeat A1c and lipid panel in three months are planned.

Walks the dog most days.

soap.assessment: Prediabetes with metabolic syndrome (central weight gain, high triglycerides, low HDL, elevated blood pressure). Allergy to lisinopril with angioedema, so no ACE inhibitors.
plan: Lifestyle changes: 150 minutes of walking a week, less sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, dietitian referral

Repeat A1c and a lipid panel in three months with return visit in three months

Doctor: Hello, and thanks for coming in. I have you down as a 46-year-old male referred for trouble with erections. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: For about eight months I have had trouble getting and keeping an erection firm enough for sex. It happens maybe two out of three times. It is embarrassing, to be honest.
Doctor: Do you still wake up with morning erections?
Patient: Yes, most mornings, so I know things still work.
Doctor: That is useful to know. Any pain, bending, or curvature of the penis during an erection?
Patient: No pain and no curve.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath when you exert yourself, or any fainting?
Patient: None of that. I jog twice a week with no chest pain and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: How are your mood and stress level?
Patient: Work has been stressful, and I worry about performing, but I do not feel depressed. Sleep is fine.
Doctor: What medications are you taking?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg once a day for blood pressure. That is my only prescription.
Doctor: Anything over the counter, like supplements?
Patient: Yes. I bought an herbal vitality product with yohimbe bark extract, two capsules before sex, and I take L-arginine 3 grams a day. I also take a multivitamin.
Doctor: Do you use nitroglycerin or any other nitrate medicine, or recreational poppers?
Patient: No nitrates and no poppers.
Doctor: Good, that matters for safety. What about alcohol and tobacco?
Patient: Two beers on weekends, and I quit smoking three years ago.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 146/92 and heart rate 78, and your BMI is 29. Your heart sounds regular without murmurs, your leg pulses are normal, and the penis and both testicles are normal with no plaques or masses. The morning total testosterone from your primary care doctor was 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin A1c 5.6 percent, and LDL 128.
Patient: So what is going on?
Doctor: My impression is erectile dysfunction, most likely from a mix of blood vessel changes and performance anxiety. Your hypertension is also above goal today. Yohimbe can raise blood pressure and cause palpitations, and neither supplement has been shown to help, so please stop the yohimbe and the L-arginine.
Patient: Okay. Is there something that works?
Doctor: Yes. I am starting sildenafil 50 mg, one tablet about an hour before sex as needed, no more than once in 24 hours. Headache, flushing, and a stuffy nose are common. Call us if an erection lasts more than four hours, and never combine it with a nitrate. Keep taking the lisinopril, and I will message your primary care doctor about the blood pressure. I also recommend counseling for the performance anxiety, regular exercise, and limiting alcohol. Let us meet again in six weeks to see how the medicine is working.
Patient: Sounds good. Thank you.
summary: A 46-year-old male was referred for erectile dysfunction of about eight months that occurs about two out of three times, with preserved morning erections. He denies penile pain or curvature, chest pain, shortness of breath, and fainting. He takes lisinopril and uses over-the-counter yohimbe bark extract and L-arginine; blood pressure was 146/92, testosterone was 412 ng/dL, and the genital exam was normal. The impression is erectile dysfunction from vascular changes and performance anxiety, with hypertension above goal. Yohimbe and L-arginine are stopped, sildenafil is started as needed, and counseling and a six-week follow-up are planned.

soap.assessment: Erectile dysfunction, most likely from vascular changes and performance anxiety. Hypertension above goal today.
plan: Stop the yohimbe and the L-arginine
Start sildenafil 50 mg, one tablet about an hour before sex as needed, no more than once in 24 hours
Counsel on side effects, to call if an erection lasts more than four hours, and never to combine sildenafil with a nitrate
Continue lisinopril and message the primary care doctor about the blood pressure
Recommend counseling for performance anxiety, regular exercise, and limiting alcohol

Doctor: I am the emergency physician. I understand you are a 57-year-old female with swelling of your lips and face. When did this start?
Patient: About two hours ago. My lips got big and tight, my eyes are puffy, and I broke out in itchy hives on my chest and arms.
Doctor: What did you eat or take today?
Patient: Nothing new to eat. I started cephalexin two days ago for a skin infection on my forearm, and this morning after a dose the hives and lip swelling started.
Doctor: Have you had any trouble breathing, wheezing, or a tight throat?
Patient: My throat feels a little scratchy, but I can swallow and breathe fine. No wheezing and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: Any vomiting, belly pain, dizziness, or fainting?
Patient: No vomiting, no belly pain, no dizziness, and no fainting.
Doctor: Any other medical problems or medicines?
Patient: I have an underactive thyroid and take levothyroxine 75 mcg every morning. Nothing else, and I have never had an allergic reaction before.
Doctor: On arrival your blood pressure was 138/82, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 98.9. You have hives across the chest and arms and swelling of the upper and lower lips. Your tongue and uvula look normal, your voice is normal, your lungs are clear, and there is no stridor. On the left forearm there is a small area of redness and warmth about 4 cm across with no pus, which is the mild cellulitis.
Patient: Is this dangerous?
Doctor: This is an allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from cephalexin, so we treat it now. I am giving epinephrine 0.3 mg intramuscular now, diphenhydramine 50 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV, and methylprednisolone 125 mg IV. I am also sending a serum tryptase level.
Patient: Okay. I feel my heart racing a bit.
Doctor: That is expected from the epinephrine. Reassessment after treatment: the hives have faded, the lip swelling is going down, your heart rate is 86, and your airway is fine. We will observe you for six hours.
Patient: What happens after that?
Doctor: If you stay stable, you go home. Stop the cephalexin now because of this reaction. You are allergic to cephalexin, so avoid it and related antibiotics from now on. For the cellulitis I am prescribing doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 7 days. You will also take prednisone 40 mg daily for 3 days and cetirizine 10 mg once daily for 5 days. I am giving you an epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg to use as needed, and I will teach you how to use it. See an allergist within a few weeks, and come back right away or call emergency services if you have trouble breathing, throat tightness, or the swelling returns.
Patient: I understand. Thank you.
summary: A 57-year-old female presented with lip and facial swelling and itchy hives that began about two hours ago, after a dose of cephalexin she started two days ago for a forearm skin infection. She denies wheezing, trouble breathing, vomiting, belly pain, dizziness, and fainting, and has an underactive thyroid on levothyroxine. Heart rate was 104 with oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, there was no stridor, and a small area of redness and warmth was on the left forearm. The impression is an allergic reaction with angioedema from cephalexin plus mild cellulitis. She received epinephrine, diphenhydramine, famotidine, and methylprednisolone, will be observed six hours, and goes home on doxycycline, prednisone, cetirizine, and an epinephrine auto-injector.

soap.subjective: Swelling of the lips and face with itchy hives on the chest and arms starting about two hours ago, after a dose of cephalexin started two days ago for a skin infection on the forearm. Throat feels a little scratchy but she can swallow and breathe. Denies wheezing, trouble breathing, vomiting, belly pain, dizziness, and fainting. Underactive thyroid on levothyroxine 75 mcg every morning. No prior allergic reactions.
soap.objective: BP 138/82, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 98.9. Hives across the chest and arms, swelling of the upper and lower lips; tongue and uvula normal, voice normal, lungs clear, no stridor. Left forearm with a small area of redness and warmth about 4 cm across and no pus. After treatment the hives faded, lip swelling decreasing, heart rate 86, airway intact.
soap.assessment: Allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from cephalexin. Mild cellulitis of the left forearm. Underactive thyroid.
plan: Epinephrine 0.3 mg intramuscular, diphenhydramine 50 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV, and methylprednisolone 125 mg IV
Serum tryptase level
Observe for six hours, then discharge home if stable
Stop cephalexin and avoid it and related antibiotics; document the allergy
Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day for 7 days for the cellulitis
Prednisone 40 mg daily for 3 days and cetirizine 10 mg once daily for 5 days
Epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg as needed with teaching on its use
Allergist follow-up within a few weeks and return precautions for breathing trouble, throat tightness, or recurrent swelling

HD#3 - 73-year-old male w/ symptomatic hyponatremia
Admitted 2d ago w/ confusion, nausea, unsteady gait x4d. 1 fall at home, no head strike per pt. Na 116 on arrival. ED gave 3% saline 100 mL bolus x1, confusion improved after.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, CAD s/p stent, BPH, CKD 3a.
Social: lives rural, no car, relies on neighbor for rides, has missed 2 clinic appts this yr. Poor access to labs near home.

Home meds (per pt + pharmacy fill hx):
- pt first stated "water pill 50 mg" daily. CORRECTION: pharmacy list shows HCTZ 25 mg daily, started 3 wks ago by PCP
- lisinopril 10 mg daily
- metformin 1000 mg BID
- atorvastatin 40 mg qHS
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- tamsulosin 0.4 mg qHS
OTC: St John's wort 300 mg TID x2 mo, fish oil 1000 mg daily. Pt never told PCP about the OTC supplements.

Interval: no overnight events. Slept ok. AAOx3 this AM. Appetite poor, eating mostly tea and toast at home (low solute intake).
Denies: CP, SOB, vomiting, seizure, abd pain, dysuria. Mild nausea persists. Still some lightheadedness on standing.

Vitals: Temp 98.2 F, BP 118/70 lying -> 100/62 standing, HR 82 -> 96, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA. Wt 71 kg (3 kg below clinic wt).
Exam: dry MM, JVP flat, no edema, lungs CTAB, RRR, abd soft NT, neuro nonfocal, no asterixis.

Labs/imaging:
Na 116 (admit) -> 123 (HD2) -> 127 today. K 3.3 -> 3.9 after repletion. Cr 1.4 (baseline 1.2), BUN 28, eGFR 49, glucose 142, Hgb 13.4.
Serum osm 248, urine osm 410, UNa 48. TSH 2.1, AM cortisol 18.
CT head: no acute process. CXR: no infiltrate. ECG: NSR, no acute changes.

A/P:
1. Symptomatic hyponatremia, hypovolemic, thiazide-induced (HCTZ) +/- low solute intake +/- St John's wort. Improving, near asymptomatic.
- HCTZ DC'd permanently, avoid thiazides in future
- St John's wort stopped, counseled pt and neighbor to stop it at home
- NS 75 mL/h x 12 h then reassess
- Na q6h, goal rise < 8 in 24h; watch for overcorrection (aquaresis) - call MD if UOP > 100 mL/h w/ fast Na rise
- liberalize diet, high-solute foods, no fluid restriction
2. HTN: BP low-normal off HCTZ w/ orthostasis. Lisinopril held tonight, resume at 5 mg daily at d/c (dose decreased from 10 mg) once Cr back to baseline.
3. T2DM: metformin decreased to 500 mg BID while inpt w/ poor PO and eGFR 49. Check FSBG before meals.
4. Hypokalemia: KCl 20 mEq PO x2 given, K now 3.9. Repeat BMP in AM.
5. AKI on CKD 3a, prerenal: Cr 1.4 vs baseline 1.2, should improve w/ volume.
6. CAD: continue aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg qHS.
7. BPH: continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg qHS, fall precautions.
8. Dispo/transport: SW and case mgmt consulted for medical transport vouchers. Home health RN to draw BMP at home in 3 days, PCP tele-visit in 1 wk instead of clinic visit. Written instructions w/ large print given to pt and neighbor. Med rec letter to PCP re HCTZ. Anticipate d/c in 24-48h if Na >= 130 and stable.
summary: A 73-year-old male with HTN, T2DM, CAD, BPH, and CKD 3a is on hospital day 3 for symptomatic hyponatremia that presented with confusion, nausea, and unsteady gait; Na was 116 on arrival and is 127 today. Pharmacy records corrected his reported water pill to HCTZ 25 mg daily, and he also used OTC St John's wort. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, vomiting, seizure, abdominal pain, and dysuria. The assessment is hypovolemic, thiazide-induced hyponatremia with low solute intake, plus AKI on CKD 3a and hypokalemia. HCTZ and St John's wort are stopped, saline and serial sodium checks continue, lisinopril is held, metformin is reduced, and transport vouchers, home lab draws, and a tele-visit are arranged.

K 3.3 then 3.9 after repletion. Cr 1.4 (baseline 1.2), BUN 28, eGFR 49, glucose 142, Hgb 13.4. Serum osm 248, urine osm 410, UNa 48, TSH 2.1, AM cortisol 18. Home meds as clarified by daughter w/ bottles:
amlodipine 5 mg daily (pt was taking BID by mistake)
alendronate 70 mg weekly
omeprazole 20 mg daily
vitamin D3 1000 IU daily
acetaminophen 500 mg PRN knee pain

note:
Nephrology progress note, hospital day 3. This 36-year-old female is 8 months status post deceased-donor kidney transplant for IgA nephropathy and was admitted with acute kidney injury after 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea from presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her creatinine on admission was 2.1 mg/dL, compared with a baseline of 1.2, and the tacrolimus trough was 14.2 ng/mL against a goal of 5 to 8. Her last scheduled lab draw was missed because she lives about 90 minutes from the transplant center and has no reliable transportation. She depends on her sister for rides, and this has led to several missed monitoring visits.

Today she feels much better. The diarrhea stopped yesterday and she is tolerating oral intake. She denies fever, dysuria, decreased urine output, pain over the graft, shortness of breath, and leg swelling.

Current medications are tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg BID, prednisone 5 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Tacrolimus was held for two doses on admission because of the elevated trough. She received lactated Ringer's at 100 mL/h overnight.

Vitals: BP 118/72, HR 80, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 98.6 F. Weight is 62 kg, up 1.5 kg from admission. She is comfortable, mucous membranes are moist, and the abdomen is soft. The graft in the right lower quadrant is non-tender without swelling. There is no peripheral edema.

Creatinine has improved from 2.1 to 1.7 yesterday and 1.4 today. BUN 31 on admission, 22 today. K 5.0 on admission and 4.4 today. Hgb 11.2. Repeat tacrolimus trough today was 9.8 ng/mL after the held doses. Urinalysis showed trace protein and no blood. BK virus PCR was negative. Renal transplant ultrasound with Doppler showed normal resistive indices, no hydronephrosis, and no fluid collection. Donor-specific antibody testing is pending.

Impression: acute kidney injury of the kidney transplant, most consistent with prerenal volume depletion from gastroenteritis combined with tacrolimus toxicity from the elevated trough, now resolving. Rejection is considered less likely, pending the donor-specific antibody result.

Plan is to restart tacrolimus at a reduced dose of 2 mg BID, down from her previous 3 mg BID, and to recheck a trough in 5 days. Continue mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg BID, prednisone 5 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Stop the IV fluids today and encourage oral hydration. Because of her transportation barriers, the transplant coordinator will arrange lab draws at an outpatient lab near her home with results sent to our team, social work will provide ride vouchers, and a telehealth visit is set for 1 week after discharge. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if creatinine continues to fall.

The impression is prerenal acute kidney injury plus tacrolimus toxicity, now resolving. Tacrolimus is restarted at 2 mg BID, other immunosuppression continues, IV fluids stop, and local lab draws, ride vouchers, and a telehealth visit are arranged.

note:
This 59-year-old male returns to cardiology clinic for follow-up of a high LDL cholesterol and statin intolerance. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and a coronary artery calcium score of 312 was obtained last year. His brother had a myocardial infarction at age 48. He developed disabling myalgias on atorvastatin 40 mg and again on rosuvastatin 5 mg, and both were stopped after the symptoms resolved within 3 weeks. He has taken no lipid-lowering medication for the last 4 months.

Today he reports no muscle pain or weakness and no dark urine. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, and lightheadedness. He is walking 30 minutes most days and has been trying to follow a Mediterranean-style diet, though he admits to frequent fast food at lunch.

His current medications are losartan 50 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, and aspirin 81 mg daily.

On exam, BP is 128/76, HR 70, weight 92 kg, and BMI 30.1. The heart is regular without murmur, the lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. There are no xanthomas. Muscle strength is 5/5 and symmetric, with no muscle tenderness.

Labs from last week show LDL 168 mg/dL off therapy, total cholesterol 245, HDL 42, triglycerides 175, CK 118 U/L which is normal, ALT 28, TSH 2.2, hemoglobin A1c 7.0 percent, and creatinine 1.0.

Impression: statin intolerance after myalgias with two different statins, with LDL 168 mg/dL. His overall risk is high given diabetes, an elevated coronary calcium score, and a family history of premature coronary disease, so the LDL goal is below 70 mg/dL. Hypertension is controlled and diabetes is at goal.

The plan is to start ezetimibe 10 mg daily and bempedoic acid 180 mg daily. I reviewed that bempedoic acid can raise uric acid and rarely cause tendon pain, and he should call if he has sudden tendon or joint pain. We will recheck a lipid panel, CK, and liver enzymes in 8 weeks. If LDL remains above 70 mg/dL at that point, we will start the process for a PCSK9 inhibitor. He will not be re-challenged with another statin at this time. Continue losartan 50 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, and aspirin 81 mg daily. Continue exercise and dietary changes, with a dietitian referral. Return to clinic in 3 months.

note: Dermatology clinic dictation. This is a 37-year-old female seen for a changing mole on the upper back. She says it has grown larger and darker over the last 6 months and itches now and then. She denies bleeding, ulceration, or pain, and she has never had skin cancer. She had several blistering sunburns as a teenager and her mother had melanoma. She lives about 2 hours from the clinic, relies on a bus, and has missed visits before because of transportation. On exam there is a 9 mm brown to black macule on the right upper back, correction, the left upper back, with an irregular border and uneven color. On dermoscopy there is an atypical network with irregular blotches. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy in the neck or axillae and no other suspicious lesions on the full skin exam. Impression is an atypical pigmented lesion, rule out melanoma. Because of her transportation barrier we did an excisional biopsy with 2 mm margins today instead of scheduling a second trip. The site was numbed with 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, 3 mL, and closed with 4-0 nylon sutures, and the specimen went to dermatopathology. Wound care is petrolatum daily with a bandage. She will get the pathology result by video visit in about 1 week, and the sutures come out in 2 weeks at a clinic near her home, with a wider excision if melanoma is confirmed. End dictation.

Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 75-year-old female here because your blood tests showed high liver enzymes. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Honestly I feel fine. A little tired sometimes, but nothing serious. My primary doctor found it on my yearly labs and said I might have a fatty liver.
Doctor: Any belly pain, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or itching?
Patient: No pain, no yellow color, no dark urine, and no itching.
Doctor: Any swelling in your legs or belly, black stools, or vomiting blood?
Patient: No swelling. No black stools, and I have not vomited blood.
Doctor: How about your weight?
Patient: I have gained about 12 pounds over the last three years.
Doctor: Do you drink alcohol?
Patient: One glass of wine on the weekends, that is all.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 20 mg once a day, lisinopril 10 mg once a day, and Tylenol 500 mg once in a while for my back.
Doctor: Any supplements or herbal products?
Patient: Yes, green tea extract capsules, 500 mg every morning, for weight loss. I started them about a year ago.
Doctor: Thank you, that is important. Today your blood pressure is 130/78, heart rate 72, weight 190 pounds, and BMI is 33. On exam your abdomen is soft and not tender, I do not feel an enlarged liver or spleen, there is no fluid in the belly, no spider veins on the skin, and no leg swelling. Your labs show ALT 78, AST 54, normal alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin 0.7, albumin 4.2, platelets 210, and INR 1.0. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody are negative, and your A1c is 6.8 percent. The ultrasound shows a bright liver consistent with fatty liver. Your FIB-4 score is 1.9, which is in the middle range, so I want to check how stiff the liver is.
Patient: Is it serious?
Doctor: My impression is elevated liver enzymes from fatty liver disease, related to your weight and diabetes, and the green tea extract may be adding to it. There are no signs of advanced scarring so far. Stop the green tea extract, because it can injure the liver. Continue the atorvastatin, which is safe with fatty liver. Limit Tylenol to no more than 2 grams a day and avoid alcohol. Aim to lose 7 to 10 percent of your body weight with a Mediterranean diet and 150 minutes of walking each week. I am ordering a FibroScan, which is a painless ultrasound test of liver stiffness, and I will repeat the liver panel in 8 weeks. We will also check your immunity to hepatitis A and B. Come back in 3 months.
Patient: That sounds manageable.
summary: A 75-year-old female was seen for elevated liver enzymes found on routine labs; she feels well apart from occasional tiredness and denies pain, yellow color, dark urine, itching, swelling, black stools, and vomiting blood. She takes metformin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and occasional Tylenol, and uses over-the-counter green tea extract for weight loss. Labs showed ALT 78 and AST 54, hepatitis B and C tests were negative, ultrasound showed fatty liver, and the FIB-4 score was 1.9. The impression is elevated liver enzymes from fatty liver disease, possibly worsened by the supplement. Green tea extract is stopped, atorvastatin continues, and a FibroScan, weight loss, acetaminophen limits, and repeat liver tests in 8 weeks are planned.
